item.title: Man charged over AI image of crocodile in Singapore reservoir
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6grveg7d9zro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Man charged over AI image of crocodile in Singapore reservoir - Published Police in Singapore have charged a man who is accused of posting an AI-generated image of a saltwater crocodile in a popular reservoir. Ye Lin was charged with communicating a false message and obstructing the course of justice for allegedly deleting the picture and the application he used. The fake image caused public concern, authorities allege. The national water agency suspended its work at the city-state's largest reservoir for two days last month after receiving information that a crocodile had been spotted. Ye Lin, who is from Myanmar, told the court through an interpreter that he intended to plead guilty, according to local media reports. The national water agency said it was alerted to a crocodile sighting in Pandan Reservoir on 20 August. Agency officials and national parks staff conducted search and capture operations in the area. The Singapore Rowing Association and Singapore Canoe Federation were told the suspend their activities. But the following day, the water agency confirmed that the crocodile image was fake and reported it to the police. The case will return to court in November and Ye Lin could face a prison sentence and a large fine if he is found guilty. In Singapore, sending a false message is punishable by up to three years in prison, a fine of up to S$10,000 (about US$7,800; £5,900), or both. Obstructing justice carries up to seven years in prison, a fine, or both. Police allege that Ye Lin created the photo of the crocodile using artificial intelligence before sending it to a colleague. "The man subsequently deleted the image and the related application in an attempt to conceal his actions," the police statement said. It is not clear how the national water agency was notified of the false photo that Ye Lin sent to his colleague.

item.title: Former American Idol contestant and pastor found guilty of murdering wife
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5rm9gv7n07xo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Former American Idol contestant and pastor found guilty of murdering wife - Published A former Ohio music pastor who once appeared on the TV talent competition American Idol has been found guilty of murdering his wife. Caleb Flynn, 40, fatally shot Ashley Flynn twice in the back of the head while she slept at their Ohio home on 16 February this year, then tried to claim that intruders had shot her. Flynn wept in court as the jury delivered its verdict after deliberating for less than three hours. He also was found guilty of the other eight charges against him, which included aggravated murder and tampering with evidence. He faces life in prison without parole. Closing arguments ended on Tuesday in Flynn's trial after eight days of testimony, which included a song played in court that prosecutors say he wrote and dedicated to the woman with whom he was having an affair. Throughout the trial, the prosecution presented evidence including police body camera footage, and activity on Flynn's iPhone and Apple Watch around the time of the murder, which took place in Tipp City, a suburb of Dayton. They also called dozens of witnesses, including his former mistress Alleigha Botner, whom he met while she was an intern at his church. Some of their 100,000 exchanged text messages were read aloud in court. The defence called no witnesses. "I was up until 4am last night crying, literally thinking of ways to kill her and not go to jail," Flynn wrote in a message to Botner, 24, in August 2025. In another message, he wrote: "I just want her dead and gone." Testifying in court, Botner said she now hates Flynn "because I believe that he murdered his wife". During closing arguments on Tuesday, prosecuting attorney Paul Watkins leaned heavily into Flynn's text exchanges, which he said demonstrated the defendant's "hatred" for his wife. He described Flynn as being afraid to lose custody of his daughters in a divorce, as well as his job with his wife's family business and his job at the church. An emotional Flynn was seen in court at times sniffling and wiping tears from his eyes. Watkins also said that when police arrived at the family home in the early hours on 16 February, Flynn told police he had been in his daughters' bedroom when he heard gunfire. Flynn said he found his 37-year-old wife dead in the bedroom, after noticing the garage side door was open. Watkins said Flynn later told investigators he had not been to the garage, contradicting his earlier statement. Flynn's defence lawyer Patrick Mulligan, meanwhile, told the court there was no concrete evidence, saying: "Connecting a couple of meaningless dots doesn't solve the case." Mulligan said the issue was not whether Flynn was a good husband to his wife, a schoolteacher and volleyball coach, and that evidence of infidelity was not evidence of murder. "They can't find the gun, therefore they blame it on him?" Mulligan questioned, referring to the charge of tampering with evidence that Flynn also faced. Flynn's gun, which had been kept in the console of his truck, has been missing since investigators arrived at the scene and found the truck's centre console open. Earlier in the trial, Botner took the stand as a witness for two days, offering testimony about her nearly 18-month relationship with Flynn. In addition to reading some of their text exchanges, she also explained the lyrics line by line from an AI-generated song. Video of the jury's reaction to the song, including what looked like laughter, went viral. Prosecutors also called Joseph Wilhelm, a special agent from Ohio's Bureau of Criminal Investigations, as a witness. He said multiple apps were uninstalled from Flynn's phone before his wife's death, including Instagram and an AI-music generating app. The music-generating app, Wilhelm said, "related to his relationship with Alleigha Botner". Flynn appeared in 2013 on the 12th series of American Idol, and sang before judges Mariah Carey, Nicki Minaj and Randy Jackson. He was featured in televised auditions, and was given a "golden ticket" to go to Hollywood, but he never reached the main competition. "Music is all I know, it's what I live to do and I love to sing, so that's why I auditioned," he said in videos shown on the programme. "Maybe my wife kinda nudged me a little, too." He is due to be sentenced on 5 October.

item.title: French hard-right leader accuses opponents of 'total war' after claims of antisemitism
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn45k85gj34o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
French hard-right leader accuses opponents of 'total war' after claims of antisemitism - Published The president of France's hard-right National Rally (RN), Jordan Bardella, has said he will sue for libel after a report published antisemitic comments that it alleged he had made as a young activist. The Mediapart website released what it said was the result of "several months" of investigation into "dozens of written conversations" Bardella allegedly had in 2013. With seven months to go before France's presidential elections, Bardella condemned "the beginnings of a total war" aimed at destabilising his party, and RN presidential candidate Marine Le Pen said she had total confidence in him. The alleged remarks included blatantly antisemitic tropes, and Bardella said they were an attempt to destroy his political career. Mediapart did not produce screen-grabs of any of the alleged remarks. It said it had "independently authenticated" the conversations, which came from "a bigger documentary base corroborated by witness statements". But Bardella, 31 – who is a likely prime minister if Le Pen wins the presidential election – said the allegations were a fabrication aimed at derailing the RN's increasingly confident bid for power. "Everything is going to be done to destabilise the campaign," he told CNews television on Monday night. "Either Mediapart is running this operation itself, or it is being manipulated by interested parties. "Of course I have instructed my lawyer to sue for libel." Le Pen said the alleged remarks "seem so weird that they can only be a forgery – one of those dirty tricks for which Mediapart appears to hold the secret". Among the statements that Mediapart alleges Bardella made when he was 17 or 18 are: "All the banks are owned by Jews"; "The Jew has to dominate other people, crush them and rob them"; and "What they want is a new world order dominated by Israel, with of course Jerusalem as its capital." Mediapart is an avowedly leftwing website which has exposed a number of scandals over the years, though its targets have been politicians of all stripes. The French hard right is riding higher than ever in pre-election polls, with the latest this week, from Toluna-Harris, showing Le Pen a clear victor over whatever rival she faces in the crucial second round in May. According to the survey, Le Pen would pick up 35-36% of the vote in the multi-candidate first round. Her likely opponent in the two-way run-off would be Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the radical left who she would eradicate with 69% of the vote. But in a stark warning for the political establishment, the poll showed that she would also easily beat the most popular centrist candidate Edouard Philippe, with a score of 57%. On Sunday the RN received another boost when results of a partial election for the upper house of parliament, the Senate, produced for the first time enough seats for the party to form an official group. Under Marine Le Pen, daughter of the historic party founder Jean-Marie Le Pen, the RN has made huge efforts to distance itself from the French far-right's antisemitic roots. Last year Bardella was the first senior figure from the party to be invited to Israel, for a conference on antisemitism. Today the party regards militant Islam as a pre-eminent threat – a position it shares with many Jews. The RN even styles itself as a "shield for the Jewish community". The alleged comments from Bardella throw back to a current of far-right thinking that Mediapart says has never been eradicated but only covered up in the new-look party. Leftwing politicians called on Bardella to resign, and the head of the Jewish umbrella organisation Crif, Yonathan Arfi, said the alleged comments "were an illustration of the limits of the RN's clean-up act". But RN deputy Jean-Philippe Tanguy said the source of the allegations was disaffected members of the party who had been expelled years ago because of their antisemitic ideas. "From what I know, it is the antisemitic rabble that were so bravely purged by Marine Le Pen. At the start of the 2010s, they were numerous and well-organised, but they were defeated. These people have always had it in for us." Related topics - Published4 September - Published11 July

item.title: Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwly5lmvy38qo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI - Published US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "giving away secrets" to America's main economic rival. Speaking at an event in Washington on Tuesday, Trump again argued against putting any restrictions on the technology that would stifle growth in the future, despite mounting public concern. Following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House last week, Beijing and Washington announced the launch of a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for November. The two countries also established a new communications channel to prevent misunderstandings during AI-related incidents. During Tuesday's event marking the launch of America.gov - a new AI-powered website designed to streamline government services - Trump argued the US was "leading by a lot" in the AI sector and did not want to "mix it up" with potential competitors. "If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. "Frankly, there is nobody in third place...it's all between us and China." Trump added that while the topic of AI came up during his meeting with President Xi last week, he remained steadfast against any sort of joint cooperation to develop the technology. "Then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know," he said, remarking that "we're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way". Prior to Trump's meeting with Xi, China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hindered AI governance. At a later White House lunch with representatives of government agencies and technology companies - including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta - Trump said among those present, there was "a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation". Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Trump said that the technology leaders had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from the potential hazards of AI. A "Super Intelligence Czar" would likely be named in the coming days, Trump added. The president signed an executive order, external on Tuesday afternoon that will formally change the name of AI to "Super Intelligence" in government documents. Domestically, Trump has faced increasing public concern over the potential dangers of AI and calls for additional guardrails to be put in place. A recent poll published by Politico in late September found that two of every three Americans believes there is at least a "moderate" risk that AI could destroy humanity. A significant portion of Trump supporters polled - 44% - said they would prefer if AI development could be paused. The US president, however, has repeatedly shrugged off safety concerns, referring to them as a "hoax" and comparing them to the "global warming scam" he claims is "being perpetrated by radical left Dumocrats". - Published23 minutes ago - Published1 day ago - Published16 September - Published22 September

item.title: Argentina threatens legal action against UK over Falkland Islands oil exploration
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq5yj1835y1wo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Argentina threatens legal action against UK over Falkland Islands oil exploration - Published Argentina's president has threatened to launch a legal challenge against the British government unless it halts oil exploration work off the coast of the Falkland Islands. In a social media post, President Javier Milei set a two-week deadline for the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between Israeli and British companies, to be scrapped. The companies insist they have valid licences issued by Britain. The comments heighten tensions between the UK and Argentina over the sovereignty of the archipelago, known in Argentina as Las Malvinas, more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982. Milei said that if the two-week deadline was not met, he had "instructed the Foreign Ministry and legal teams to initiate international arbitration" against the UK over what he called "the illegal plundering of our resources through the Sea Lion Project". He continued to warn the UK that if the "illegitimate exploitation" of the region didn't end within two weeks, Argentina would take the matter before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. The International Tribunal is an independent judicial body based in Hamburg which is responsible for the fair application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea. The move comes soon after Milei roundly criticised the UN in his speech at the General Assembly for failing to act over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands. He said the UN had become "a useless organisation" which only serves "arrogant parasites dressed up as well-intentioned bureaucrats". Since then, the UK Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, said that Argentina "lacks the ability" to seize the Falklands by force. Milei had previously said the Sea Lion oilfield was a "clear and present danger". The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil. Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years. Both companies have in the past stressed that Sea Lion holds valid licences from the Falkland Islands. In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against. Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them. The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel. Related topics - Published8 September - Published18 September

item.title: Hurricane Polo makes landfall on Mexico's Pacific coast
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8d3z5y7958o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Hurricane Polo makes landfall on Mexico's Pacific coast - Published Hurricane Polo has made landfall along the northern Pacific coast of Mexico, lashing the state of Baja California Sur with life-threatening winds and heavy rain that has already flooded some coastal areas. Mexican officials said Polo moved ashore just south of the surfing and fishing village of Las Barrancas bringing maximum sustained winds of 110 mph (175 km/h). Polo is moving northeast and on the forecast track, its core is predicted to continue passing over Baja California Sur before moving inland over the southern part of the Mexican state of Sonora later on Tuesday. Residents in threatened areas have been encouraged to seek shelter. Shopkeeper María Palomino, 57, spent the night at a high school which has been turned into a temporary shelter. "If something happens, it's better to come to the shelter," she told AFP news agency. A whale-watching and fishing guide who was boarding up the facade of his home told AFP the storm was "coming with full force". The US-based National Hurricane Center (NHC) said that while Polo was expected to weaken as it moved over the Baja California peninsula, it was forecast to still be at hurricane strength when it makes its second landfall in mainland Mexico. Meteorologists said Polo could dump between 6 and 12 inches (150-300mm) of rain across parts of Baja California Sur, which they warned could produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain. The NHC said a storm surge was also expected to produce significant coastal flooding in areas of onshore winds. "Near the coast, the surge will be accompanied by large and destructive waves," it said in an update. Even before Polo made landfall, residents said there were power cuts in Baja California Sur. US media reported some flooding in the fishing town of Puerto San Carlos and the Associated Press said waves crested sea barriers in the area, where many residents had been evacuated due to the threat. Meteorologists said dangerous surf and rip currents were likely to continue along portions of the north-western coast of Mexico and Baja California for the next day or so. The south of the peninsula is popular with tourists and acts as a base for surfers, sport fishers, and whale watchers. In Cabo San Lucas, famous for its natural rock arch, authorities had restricted access to the beaches on Monday. Polo has been slowly moving towards Mexico's coast line for days. Meteorologists said it was being fuelled by extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon, which has led to a more active hurricane season in Pacific waters. As Polo moves north-east, it is expected to also affect the US, sending a surge of tropical moisture northwards for the next few days leading to excessive rainfall and flash flooding. Rain has already been falling across Arizona and California but the remains of Polo and another hurricane - named Odalys - will become absorbed into that weather system, boosting the amount of rainfall. These fronts will push eastwards across the southern plains. Some spots could see as much as 6 or 7 inches of rainfall by Thursday. States affected include Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Utah into Tuesday. Related topics - Published22 September - Published6 days ago

item.title: Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjkg7k6z9296o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign - Published Like thousands of other residents of Zaporizhzhia, Denys Maksyshko has spent years working for local steel factory Zaporizhstal. For generations, it has been the biggest and richest source of employment in this major Ukrainian city. "Zaporizhstal is not just a big company, it's the heart of the city," he says. Now, following a series of Russian missile strikes, this heart has stopped beating. The huge factory that employs 8,500 people shut down indefinitely after four waves of Russian attacks - two in August, and two in September. "All the equipment has been almost completely destroyed. There are no windows left, and there are holes in the roofs. The blast furnaces have been almost completely ruined," Maksyshko complains. Russia fired a total of 17 missiles at Zaporizhstal, according to Oleksandr Myronenko, chief operating officer of steelworks owner Metinvest. Eight workers were killed and 31 wounded. "We're now clearing rubble and trying to plan recovery," Myronenko tells the BBC. At the moment it is far from certain Zaporizhstal will ever start up again. Russia's persistent campaign of air strikes against Ukrainian metallurgical plants started in August. By now, all of them have been hit, some several times. This is a key sector of the Ukrainian economy, and naturally an attractive target for Russia. Before the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's GDP and a third of its exports. It provided employment for more than half a million people, and every 13th job in Ukraine was linked to the industry one way or another. Because of the recent Russian attacks, it has all but ground to a halt and its contribution to Ukraine's GDP now "is probably close to zero", says Myronenko. Until recently his company was Ukraine's biggest producer of steel and iron, but all its steelworks are for now out of action. "Clearly, they're trying to stop Ukraine's economy and stop Ukraine from getting [export] money from abroad, from paying taxes and wages, from ensuring that cities live and people have jobs," says Myronenko. "Their efforts have been very effective so far." The damage to the metals industry could have devastating consequences for Ukraine's economy and society. Ukraine had 12 metallurgical plants before losing parts of its industrial heartland in the east shortly after the start of hostilities with Russia in 2014. By 2018, there were just nine, and three years into the full-scale war in 2025 that number had fallen to six. Among those lost were the Azovstal and Illich plants in Mariupol, Ukraine's south-eastern city captured after a months-long Russian siege. Among the steel-making cities caught up in Russia's recent missile campaign is President Volodymyr Zelensky's home city of Kryvyi Rih. On 25 September, Ukraine's biggest steelworks, Arcelor Mittal Kryvyi Rih, announced it was unable to reopen after repeated attacks over five weeks, praising the bravery of its workers, five of whom had died. Latest on war in Ukraine - Cultural treasures are being destroyed worldwide - so why is no-one being punished? - Published20 September Local Defence Council head Oleksandr Vilkul issued an emergency address to the city's residents, in which he spoke of a "very serious blow" that would affect more than just thousands of jobs. The situation, he admitted, was very difficult. "It is taxes feeding into our community's budget," he said. "They provided funds for keeping the city's infrastructure running, repairing heating plants and their pipes, funds for nursery schools, social services and many other things." Taxes paid by metal-making companies have funded 30-70% of local government spending in their host cities, says Stanislav Zinchenko, head of Kyiv-based consultancy GMK Center. "In other words, the physical survival of these cities depended on these companies," he told the BBC. "This is a catastrophic problem for Ukraine's economy. Before the war, the mining and metallurgical industry was a key industry," he told the BBC. "It was always the biggest investor in the economy, investing $2bn-$3bn (£1.5bn-£2.3bn) a year on average." If the steelworks remain shut, hundreds of thousands of people may lose their jobs, and the resulting waves of migration will reach far beyond Ukraine, Zinchenko warned. "A humanitarian catastrophe is looming." The end of steelmaking in Ukraine would also have severe consequences for its defence capabilities and reconstruction. Steel is vital for producing military equipment, as well as for making shelters and repairing countless buildings damaged by Russia. Russia has justified its attacks on the steel plants for that reason, alleging that the plants in Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih were all producing military hardware. "We attempted relaunching Zaporizhstal. We restarted a furnace, and it worked for 10 hours before there was another air strike," Oleksandr Vodoviz of Metinvest told a conference in Kyiv. There was no point yet on spending money on recovery as the situation was unclear, he added. Even if production were to resume, it would not be business as usual for Ukrainian steelmakers any time soon. Russian attacks on railways have made transporting their products within Ukraine difficult and dangerous, and strikes against ports have turned exports into a lethal lottery. "Ports have essentially been blocked," said Oleksandr Myronenko. "Every ship is at risk of being attacked, and their chances are 50-50 - either you make it, or you don't." EU quotas on steel imports introduced on 1 July may compound the problems faced by Ukraine. But Denys Maksyshko, the Zaporizhstal worker, remains upbeat. His colleagues are doing their bit to revive the factory, clearing away rubble and fixing whatever can be fixed. "This is similar to what the military do in the trenches. Ordinary people are fighting to keep the factory alive like soldiers."

item.title: The Frenemy: How Australia navigates superpower rivalry
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c61wxyzr4rwyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The Frenemy: How Australia navigates superpower rivalry - Published Snipers shatter the silence of the Australian bush. Then the missiles hit, the smoke rising in the distance. The buzz of drones starts up, soon to be drowned out by helicopters flying overhead. Every piece of hardware is being deployed, no expense spared. But this is no war zone – the last time Townsville saw conflict was during World War Two. This is a show of military might. " We live in a volatile world," says Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan. "Training an army to be prepared to fight a war that is potentially more likely than it has been previously, [is] very important." War is no longer an abstract concept for Australians who often feel removed from the problems facing other parts of the world. Thousands of miles from active conflict, the country, like everywhere else, is facing the knock-on effects of Iran and Ukraine such as higher fuel prices and rising inflation. With China's military capabilities also on the rise and its increasing influence in the Pacific, there's also more concern about the threat it represents. Australia has responded by deepening its relationship with the US, its security ally and China's rival superpower. But that also puts Australia in a tricky position - for China's rise has also given Australia its biggest trading partner. It's a paradox that most people are well aware of - which is probably why we've been invited to report on what Australia is doing to protect itself but nobody is willing to say whom they're preparing to fight. "We're rehearsing for a war - the worst type of war - a World War Two-like war, a World War One-type war, a total war," says Brigadier McLennan, preferring to remain vague when asked who the enemy is. Binding tighter to the US The war scenario playing out before us is part of a major joint exercise known as "Southern Jackaroo" - a training programme involving the Australian, American and Japanese armed forces aimed at strengthening defence co-operation across the Indo-Pacific. "We like to call ourselves America's 911 response force," US Marine Kevin Hicks says. And in terms of numbers, they are more prepared than ever. In 2012, just 200 US Marines were deployed to Australia for an annual six-month deployment. Today, that figure has risen to around 2,500. A quick read of Australia's 2026 National Defence Strategy gives you an easy answer as to why these numbers are growing. "Intense competition between major powers – principally the United States and China – will be an enduring feature of our strategic environment," it said. "China continues to undertake the largest military build-up in the world today, without the transparency or strategic reassurance the region expects." The military tie-ups aren't just being seen in terms of troops but in bases too - most obviously in the north of the country such as RAAF Tindal air base in the Northern Territory which has been upgraded to support long-range American B52 bombers. But the security partnership between the US, the UK and Australia - Aukus - arming Australia with nuclear submarines, is arguably the biggest example of deepening ties. The Australian approach differs from that of its fellow middle powers. While Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has talked about middle powers reorganising their priorities in light of an increasingly unreliable US, Australia seems to be intent on tying itself ever closer. But that comes as Australians themselves increasingly doubt their relationship with the US. "Only 31% of Australians trust the United States to act responsibly in the world, and a mere 28% of Australians trust China to do the same," says Charles Lyons-Jones, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute, citing their annual poll. "Those are striking findings when you consider the level of trust that the Australian government has with the United States." The 'frenemy' While Australia's alliance with the US is changing, so too is its relationship with China. Armed forces might be prepping for a potential military conflict but the fact remains China is Australia's most important economic partner. Australia and China have had diplomatic relations since 1972 but it was only in the early 2010s that China became Australia's biggest trading partner, hungry for all the commodities it had to offer. Australia opened up its economy and encouraged business and trade, Chinese President Xi Jinping was invited to address parliament. And it culminated in the signing of a free trade agreement in 2015. The golden era didn't last long though. When Australia suggested an investigation into the origins of Covid in 2020, China objected to this line of questioning and retaliated with tariffs. And then in 2021, Australia became the first nation to perform a U-turn on China's Belt and Road Initiative - its massive global infrastructure plan - when they cancelled the state of Victoria's agreement with the Chinese government three years after signing up. A number of Australians have also been detained in China, including journalist Cheng Lei, who was released in 2023 after more than three years. Relations have improved in recent years under the Labor government of Anthony Albanese, but it's not without challenges. In June this year for example, China slapped 55% tariffs on beef to protect its own domestic market - despite the free trade agreement. Even with these hiccups, this year's Lowy Institute Poll found that a majority of Australians (61%) saw China more as an economic partner than a security threat. That was an 11-point increase from last year. When it comes to China investing in Australia though, they are more wary. "There are a number of European countries which are larger investors in Australia than China, and that is because our jurisdictions are much more similar, and there is a greater level of trust between our governments," says Lyons-Jones. This year's Lowy Institute Poll also showed that for the first time, a majority of Australians (51%) believed that Australia's relationship with China was more important than its relationship with the US. Rise and fall of superpowers Earlier this month, former Prime Minister Kevin Rudd – a fluent Mandarin speaker - gave an address in which he talked of "radical changes" now reshaping Australia's national security, including "the rise and rise of China at a time when America continues to debate what sort of global power it wants to be". Dr Marina Yue Zhang, an Associate Professor at the University of Technology Sydney agrees Australia's relationship with its closest ally is changing. "The US is really doing something dramatic and more and more people in Australia - and I think globally - have realised 'is this the big brother we can all trust and put all our faith in?' " she says. But old rivalries live on. With Australia caught between two superpowers, every exchange between their leaders carries weight. And in Beijing earlier this year, when Xi met Trump, the Chinese president invoked the idea of the "Thucydides Trap", the theory that conflict can become almost inevitable when a rising power challenges an established one. "This is, if not the transition of great powers, at least [it's] power struggles of great powers, says Zhang. And in that competition, Australia is inevitably affected. The US is a security ally that while more unreliable than in the past is still its mainstay. But economically so too is China. It's not an either/or relationship, it's a balancing act. "There's no way Australia will choose one side and [dump] the other- it's not in their interests," Zhang says. "It's getting harder and harder to maintain, but Australia has to do it."

item.title: How an alleged rape sent an Indian university into turmoil and emptied hostels
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6kg8dxrv54do?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How an alleged rape sent an Indian university into turmoil and emptied hostels - Published One of India's largest private universities has suspended classes after an unverified allegation that a female student was raped on campus set off protests that descended into violence. Police say they have registered a case and are trying to verify whether last week's alleged rape at Lovely Professional University (LPU) did happen. The university has categorically denied the allegation. Police say no student has come forward to say she was assaulted, investigators have yet to identify the alleged victim or the perpetrator, and CCTV footage examined so far has yielded no evidence of an attack. But rumours on student WhatsApp groups led to unrest over the weekend at the sprawling 600-acre university in Punjab that draws students from India and abroad. Founded in 2005 by a family whose business began with a small sweet shop, LPU has grown into a largely self-contained world of hostels and lecture halls, with thousands of young people living on campus. Images and videos showed vehicles in flames, crowds filling a major highway and police wielding canes as unrest spilled beyond the university gates. Police vehicles were damaged, officers injured and parts of the campus was vandalised. By Monday, the highway had reopened and the campus was calmer, but heavily policed. University authorities described the claims circulating on social media as false and baseless, but it did little to reassure students with hostels emptying within hours. Key exams were postponed and students were allowed to go home. Following demands from protesting students, police registered a rape case against "an unidentified person" and formed a seven-member special investigation team, or SIT, to investigate. What happened? The unrest began in the early hours of 27 September, when word spread that a female student had been raped in or near one of the university's hostels a few days earlier. The suspect was variously described - by students and in media reports - as a plumber, painter or construction worker. Some students said the assault had occurred on 23 September and accused the university of failing to act after being informed. BBC Punjabi found that messages about the allegation had circulated through WhatsApp groups. As they travelled, crowds gathered. Hundreds eventually spilled on to National Highway 44, a major route between Delhi and Punjab, blocking traffic for more than 15 hours. By Sunday evening, university property had been damaged, objects set alight and stones thrown at police vehicles. Videos showed police striking protesters with canes, although police later denied carrying out a baton-charge. Behind the gates, students described a night of fear. "We were sitting with knives and scissors," Arya, a student, told BBC Punjabi. Students had been told to lock themselves inside their rooms, she said, while people knocked on their doors. "We were just thinking that somehow this night would pass and we would get out of here." Police later arrived and made them feel safer, she said. By the next day, she wanted to leave. "Our parents also want us to just get out of here." So why have police lodged a case? That the police open a case and investigate the allegation was among the protesters' central demands. "The students have been demanding that an FIR [First Information Report] is to be registered, but the students could not provide us with any victim's name," senior police official Naveen Singla told the BBC. Police nevertheless registered an FIR under India's rape law against an unidentified person. An FIR formally records an allegation for investigation; it does not establish that a crime occurred. Singla said investigators had also begun examining CCTV footage. The preliminary search, he told the BBC, had so far shown no outsider entering a room. "As of now, it can't be verified that rape has happened or not," he said. But they are continuing to examine the footage. "The campus is quite large, so we haven't been able to see all the cameras yet," Sinha told reporters on Monday. "We have initially checked the places that the students had mentioned, but we will get to the bottom of this." Why did the protests grow so large? It is difficult to say. What began with an allegation of rape quickly became a broader protest over security, the university's response and, eventually, the violence itself. There was also growing uncertainty over who was on the campus. Some students insisted the demonstrations had begun peacefully and blamed outsiders for at least some of the violence. Others told BBC Punjabi of seeing masked or unfamiliar people inside the university. "We were really scared," said Pawan, a student. "It became a complete battlefield." Another student, Aniket Singh, said outsiders had entered a women's hostel and knocked on doors claiming to be police officers. Police have since confirmed that outsiders were among the crowds, but said they were still trying to establish who they were and what role they played. Amid that confusion, the university's attempt to dispel the rape allegation produced a controversy of its own. On Monday, LPU released a video of three women living in the hostel room that had been linked to the alleged assault. They said nothing had happened there and asked people to stop disturbing them. The same students later alleged in another video that university officials had instructed them what to say, edited the recording and posted it without their consent. Those claims have not been independently verified. LPU has not commented on the students' allegations. Another claim circulating during the protests sought to connect the alleged rape with the recent suicide of a female LPU student from Telangana state. Police say investigations into her death had already begun and there is no verified evidence linking the two cases. What is happening now? For now, life on campus has been interrupted. Regular classes have been suspended for 10 days and exams postponed. Students have been asked to return home after consulting their parents or guardians. Those who are staying have been advised to stay in their residences and avoid further unrest. The Punjab State Women's Commission has also sought the FIR, details of the investigation and information about arrangements for students' safety. The investigation now has two separate questions to answer: whether there is evidence of the assault that set the protests in motion? And who was responsible for the violence that followed? Addressing the students on Monday, LPU's pro-chancellor Rashmi Mittal said she was hurt that despite the university's many channels for students to raise concerns, they had instead "believed the rumour that was spreading". She also alleged that outsiders had joined the unrest. "I feel students can't do this," she said. item.title: Journalist crowned king in Uganda after bitter succession dispute
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx7v4glz50elo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Journalist crowned king in Uganda after bitter succession dispute - Published Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma has been crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom. The new monarch has long been a familiar face in the East African nation, where for many he was known not as the heir to the throne, but as a storyteller: a long-serving anchor and editor at the state broadcaster. But the 56-year-old - now King Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo I - has become the subject of media attention himself as his rise to the Tooro throne sparked controversy and widespread reactions beyond the country. Tooro is one of Uganda's four main officially recognised historical kingdoms. For the last 31 years, it had been headed by King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who was once known as a "boy king", after ascending to the throne as an infant. Oyo became king in 1995 at the age of just three, following the death of his father. Then the world's youngest monarch, he ruled until he died last month from cancer, aged just 34. The coronation is a day for celebration, involving traditional practices that started at midnight. Kijanangoma has had to perform various ceremonies and walk about 4km (2.5 miles) to the official Karuziika royal palace where he has now been crowned. The Tooro kingdom's Information Minister Charles Mwanguhya told the BBC Focus on Africa podcast that a mock fight would follow his crowning, to signify that kingship does not come easy. Kijanangoma would then be blessed by members of the royal Babiito clan, he said. But his selection was far from straightforward. According to tradition, a recognised son of the late king should have succeeded him. Close members of the royal family said Oyo had left a young son and a will with instructions that the child should be next on the throne. But the son has never been revealed to the public and nor was he recognised by the committee of 21 Babiito clan members who choose the king and eventually selected Kijanangoma. The late King Oyo was never publicly married, and little is known about his wife or their son. Nonetheless his mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, argued that the late king's will ought to have been respected. However, the royal succession committee ignored her wishes, insisting their selection process was conducted in accordance with Tooro customs and traditions. The new king has thus found himself at the centre of a succession dispute, with Kemigisa and her close relatives unhappy with the outcome. Kemigisa referred to Kijanangoma's selection as the "announcement of a second king" being "made after the will of King Oyo was read to members of the royal family". "As a mother, that was extraordinarily painful," she said, describing celebrations for the next king taking place "only metres from where my son's body lay". The queen later said Oyo's son, who was in the US state of Texas, had been due to return home but that could not happen amid a "tense and polarised succession dispute". "No child should be placed in circumstances where returning to his father's homeland could mean being drawn into hostility and conflict," Kemigisa asserted in a post on X. But according to the Tooro kingdom's information minister, the son being talked about "hasn't been presented anywhere, which means there is a growing acceptance that sad as it may be, King Oyo didn't leave a son behind". While King Oyo inherited the crown from his father, Mwanguhya told the BBC "the crown has moved to a different line within the ruling clan". A king must come from the Babiito clan, specifically the lineage of King George David Matthew Kamurasi Rukidi III, according to royal palace sources. Kijanangoma and the late King Oyo are cousins. Both are grandsons of Rukidi III, the 11th king, or Omukama, who ruled the Tooro kingdom from 1928 to 1965. Kijanangoma was among several people who were considered for the role, including Prince George Desmond Kamurasi, who plays football for one of the UK's best-known amateur clubs. According to the succession committee, the South East Dons captain and goalkeeper declined the offer of the throne, citing other responsibilities. After he was formally announced, Kijanangoma promised that the palace would be open to the people, while vowing to focus on unity and development. "I ask you for one thing - they have given me this title as king but I cannot work alone, I have to work with you," he said. Uganda's traditional kings have no formal political authority, but they retain cultural influence and command significant loyalty in the communities they lead. The country is home to four main kingdoms, the largest and most prominent being Buganda in the central region, which encompasses the capital Kampala. The kingdoms were abolished in 1967, but the government under President Yoweri Museveni restored them in the early 1990s. The government said this was to promote cultural pride and national unity, but the move has also been interpreted as a way of appeasing communities and fostering political loyalty. Amid the succession dispute, the government backed the Babiito clan's choice of Kijanangoma. Attorney General Sam Mayanja said the Tooro kingdom was cleared to go ahead with the coronation, as there had not been a formal complaint against him. The date of the coronation was announced by the government with President Museveni attending the ceremony. The president's son and the head of the military, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, has also publicly supported Kijanangoma. "Long may he reign," he posted on X. Kijanangoma's very name points to his royal heritage. His father, the first Kijanangoma, was born in the year King Rukidi III became king. The king gave him the name, which means the "one who comes with the royal drum". The drum of royalty, foretold two generations earlier, is now returning to its bearer. Kijanangoma was born in 1970 and raised at their family home at Kidukuru village in Fort Portal, about 300km (186 miles) from Kampala. He left the village to pursue further studies and graduated with a mass communication degree from Uganda's prestigious Makerere University in 1999. He worked as a broadcaster in a career spanning more than two decades, including in neighbouring Rwanda and at home, with the Uganda Broadcasting Corporation (UBC). The years spent engaging with the public, the interactions with leaders and the exposure to national affairs in his work as a journalist may yet serve him well as he returns to the community he came from, this time as their leader. After he was named king, Kijanangoma said he would use the connections he had built up over 21 years working as a journalist "to get good things for our people". His mother, Assimwe Yusta Kijanangoma, is confident that he is well prepared for his new role. She says his upbringing was deeply rooted in tradition. "I really raised him with the teachings of the old kingdom of a cane and instructions and scolding. I laugh with him, and other times I scold him," she told the BBC. She added: "Eddy is well-mannered, he does not fight, or shout, even when wronged, he says a few words and does not go so much into it." She feels good for her son, although she admits to having mixed emotions, especially as her son is taking over after the death of a "great man". Watch: Moment a government building collapses into a river in Nepal amid floods Massive flooding left a government building in western Nepal teetering on the edge of an unstable ledge before it fell into the Daram River. Witnesses captured the moment that the building in Baglung collapsed on Sunday, 27 September. Officials removed important documents and computers from the building before it fell, local ward chair Tej Thapa confirmed to the BBC. No one was injured. Landslides and floods have killed at least 27 people over recent days, according to Nepal's national disaster agency, only weeks after a flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border killed 1,400 people and left thousands more missing. Fires and blockades as students stage school protests across France More than 400 people, most of them children, were arrested in France on Tuesday during a wave of school protests across the country. The country's interior minister Laurent Nuñez told broadcaster BFMTV that 440 people in total had been detained, while 48 law enforcement members had been injured. Students are demonstrating over issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages. France's education ministry said 400 schools were impacted by protests or disruptions on Tuesday. The movement at French lycées, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Île-de-France region around Paris. The protests on Tuesday came the same day as professionals from public sectors - including teachers and firefighters - also demonstrated against planned budget cuts in France. Close-up look at Turner's '£50m' Rome painting on show in the city A renowned painting by British landscape artist JMW Turner has returned to the city that inspired it nearly two centuries ago. Rome, from Mount Aventine features a panoramic view of the Italian capital and will be on display at the Palazzo Rondinini for three days. Dating back to the 19th century, the masterpiece was based on sketches made in Rome. The work of art is remarkably well preserved and is believed to have never been restored. It even features traces of fingerprints and brush hairs are still visible. The painting has only been to auction once before, selling for more than £30 million. Sotheby's now expects it could fetch around £50 million when it goes under the hammer in London this December. The BBC's Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Sarah Rainsford, had a close-up look at the painting in Rome. Watch: US journalist Evan Gershkovich describes being detained by Russian agents US journalist Evan Gershkovich has told the BBC's Today programme about the 16 months when he was detained in Russia. In his first UK broadcast interview, the Wall Street Journal correspondent said he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in March 2023, and arrested him. He was later sentenced to 16 years on espionage charges, but released in 2024 as part of a high-profile prisoner exchange. He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false, and following his arrest, then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home. Watch: From launch to fiery splashdown, SpaceX's Starship completes orbit test SpaceX's Starship rocket has splashed down in the Pacific Ocean after orbiting the Earth for about three hours. The mission was supposed to last about 10 hours, but the SpaceX team decided to end it early. The ship deployed 26 "next generation" Starlink V3 satellites, joining the existing constellation which deliver broadband internet on Earth. SpaceX describes Starship as "the world's most powerful launch vehicle ever developed" and says it will eventually carry crew and cargo "to Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars and beyond". The aim of the spacecraft is to be able to carry up to 100 people on "long-duration, inter-planetary flights".
